items.title: When SHA-1 broke
items.claim: In 2017 Google and CWI announced 'SHAttered', the first practical collision in SHA-1. About how much computation did it take?
items.reveal_title: Thousands of CPU-years to break SHA-1
items.reveal:
The 2017 SHAttered attack required roughly 6,500 CPU-years of computation. By 2020 the SHA-1 chosen-prefix attack (Leurent and Peyrin) cost about $45,000 on rented GPUs.

SHA-1 is now deprecated in major standards.
items.why: Cryptographic 'breaks' become economic problems before they become practical attacks.

items.title: 0.1 + 0.2 in IEEE 754
items.claim: In most programming languages using IEEE 754 double-precision arithmetic, what does 0.1 + 0.2 evaluate to?
items.reveal:
Neither 0.1 nor 0.2 has an exact binary representation. The standard IEEE 754 double evaluates the sum to 0.30000000000000004.

Decimal or arbitrary-precision libraries are used where this matters (finance, audit).
items.why: Numerical errors emerge from representation, not arithmetic mistakes.

items.title: Stateful firewalls track connections, not just packets
items.claim: A stateful firewall differs from a stateless packet filter how?

options.text: Stateful firewalls remember active connections; replies on established TCP sessions are allowed without re-evaluation against rules. Stateless filters evaluate each packet independently

items.reveal:
Cisco PIX (1994) was an early commercial stateful firewall. Tracking connection state allows simpler rules: 'allow outbound, allow replies to outbound' instead of complex bidirectional packet rules.

Deep packet inspection (DPI) firewalls go further, examining application-layer content. Next-generation firewalls (NGFW) combine stateful filtering with intrusion prevention, application identification and TLS inspection. Cloud-native firewalls (security groups, NSGs) typically operate at L4 statefully.
items.why: The shift from packet to connection awareness made firewalls usable in practice. Modern systems extend this to application awareness.
